nodes.name: Transpose, conjugate and conjugate transpose notation
nodes.statement: Given a complex matrix $\matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$, we denote by $\matr{Z}^{{\sf T}}$, $\matr{Z}^{*}$ and $\matr{Z}^{{\sf H}}$ its \emph{transpose, conjugate} and \emph{conjugate transpose,} respectively.

nodes.name: Diamond transpose notation
nodes.statement: We shall also use $(\cdot)^{{\blacklozenge}}$ to denote either $(\cdot)^{{\sf T}}$ or $(\cdot)^{{\sf H}}$.

nodes.name: Hermitian matrix
nodes.statement: A complex matrix $\matr{A}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ is called \emph{Hermitian} if $\matr{A}^{{\sf H}}=\matr{A}$.

nodes.name: Complex symmetric matrix
nodes.statement: It is called \emph{complex symmetric} if $\matr{A}^{{\sf T}}=\matr{A}$.

nodes.name: Set of target matrices A^(l)
nodes.statement: Let $\{\matr{A}^{(\ell)}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq \matrelem{L}}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ be a set of complex matrices.

nodes.name: Blind source separation (BSS) problem
nodes.statement: The well-known \emph{blind source separation} (BSS) problem \cite{Como94:sp,Como10:book,maurandi2014decoupled,souloumiac2009nonorthogonal} can be formulated as finding a full column rank matrix $\matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$ to make the matrices $\matr{W}^{(\ell)}=\matr{Z}^{{\blacklozenge}}\matr{A}^{(\ell)} \matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$ simultaneously as diagonal as possible.
nodes.statement_short: Find a full column rank Z making all Z^♦ A^(l) Z simultaneously as diagonal as possible.
nodes.origin_citation: Comon 1994; Comon & Jutten 2010; Maurandi et al. 2014; Souloumiac 2009

nodes.name: Joint approximate diagonalization of matrices (JADM) problem
nodes.statement: A natural idea is to solve the \emph{joint approximate diagonalization of matrices} (JADM) problem, which consists in minimizing \begin{equation} f(\matr{Z}) = \sum_{\ell=1}^{\matrelem{L}} \|\offdiag{\matr{W}^{(\ell)}}\|^2, \end{equation} where $\matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$ is a full column rank matrix, and $\offdiag{\cdot}$ is the \emph{zero diagonal} operator, setting all the diagonal elements of a square matrix in $\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$ to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the sum of squared off-diagonal norms of Z^♦ A^(l) Z over full column rank Z.

nodes.name: JADM cost function f(Z)
nodes.statement: f(\matr{Z}) = \sum_{\ell=1}^{\matrelem{L}} \|\offdiag{\matr{W}^{(\ell)}}\|^2,
nodes.label: eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0

nodes.name: Ill-posedness of JADM over full-column-rank matrices
nodes.statement: Note that, the set of full-column rank matrices is not closed (the limit of a sequence of full column rank matrices can be rank deficient), and therefore problem \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0} is ill-posed. For example, for a full column rank matrix $\matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$ and nonzero $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$, we have $\lim_{\lambda\to 0}f(\lambda\matr{Z}) = \lim_{\lambda\to 0} |\lambda|^4f(\matr{Z}) =0$.
nodes.statement_short: Full column rank matrices do not form a closed set, so f(λZ)→0 as λ→0 and the problem is ill-posed.

nodes.name: JADM-H, JADM-CS and JADM-RS special cases
nodes.statement: Problem \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0} has been widely used in BSS and \emph{Independent component analysis} (ICA) \cite{chabriel2014joint,Como10:book,Afsa07:honolulu,andre2018new}, and has the following well-known special cases: \begin{itemize} \item \emph{joint approximate diagonalization of Hermitian matrices} (JADM-H) \cite{sorensen2009approximate,maurandi2014decoupled}: $(\cdot)^{{\blacklozenge}}=(\cdot)^{{\sf H}}$, $\matr{A}^{(\ell)} \in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ is Hermitian for $1\leq\ell\leq \matrelem{L}$; \item \emph{joint approximate diagonalization of complex symmetric matrices} (JADM-CS) \cite{maurandi2014decoupled}: $(\cdot)^{{\blacklozenge}}=(\cdot)^{{\sf T}}$, $\matr{A}^{(\ell)} \in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ is complex symmetric for $1\leq\ell\leq \matrelem{L}$; \item \emph{joint approximate diagonalization of real symmetric matrices} (JADM-RS) \cite{afsari2004gradient,afsari2006simple}: over real $\matr{Z}$, $(\cdot)^{{\blacklozenge}}=(\cdot)^{{\sf T}}$, $\matr{A}^{(\ell)} \in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is real symmetric for $1\leq\ell\leq \matrelem{L}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Special cases of JADM: Hermitian (JADM-H), complex symmetric (JADM-CS) and real symmetric (JADM-RS) target matrices.
nodes.origin_citation: Sorensen et al. 2009; Maurandi et al. 2014; Afsari 2004, 2006

nodes.name: General and special linear groups
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\{\matr{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}, {\rm det}(\matr{X})\neq 0\}$ (resp. $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\{\matr{X}\in\mathbf{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}), {\rm det}(\matr{X})=1\}$) be the \emph{general} (resp. \emph{special}) \emph{linear group}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem

nodes.name: Rectangular special linear set RSL(m,n,C)
nodes.statement: We define the \emph{rectangular special linear set} as \begin{align} \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) \stackrel{\sf def}{=} \{\matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}, \matr{Z}^{{\sf H}}\matr{Z}\in\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem

nodes.name: Definition of RSL(m,n,C)
nodes.statement: \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) \stackrel{\sf def}{=} \{\matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}, \matr{Z}^{{\sf H}}\matr{Z}\in\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem
nodes.label: eq:def_rsl

nodes.name: RSL is closed and consists of full column rank matrices
nodes.statement: Every matrix in $\textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ is of full column rank, and, moreover this set is closed.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem
conclusions: Every matrix in $\textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ is of full column rank

nodes.name: Complex Stiefel manifold St(m,n,C)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) \stackrel{\sf def}{=}\{\matr{Y}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}, \matr{Y}^{{\sf H}}\matr{Y}= \matr{I}_m\}$ be the \emph{complex Stiefel manifold}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem

nodes.name: RSL factorization lemma
nodes.statement: A complex matrix $\matr{Z}\in\textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ if and only if there exist $\matr{Y}\in\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ and $\matr{X}\in\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ such that $\matr{Z}=\matr{Y}\matr{X}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem
conclusions: A complex matrix $\matr{Z}\in\textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ if and only if there exist $\matr{Y}\in\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ and $\matr{X}\in\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ such that $\matr{Z}=\matr{Y}\matr{X}$
nodes.statement_short: Z is in RSL iff Z = YX with Y in the Stiefel manifold and X in SL_m.
nodes.label: lem:rela-equiavalent

nodes.name: JADM on St(m,n,C) x SL_m(C) (first reformulation)
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lem:rela-equiavalent}, problem \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0} over $\textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ is equivalent to minimizing \begin{equation} f: \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\times\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+},\ \ (\matr{Y},\matr{X})\mapsto \sum_{\ell=1}^{\matrelem{L}} \|\offdiag{\matr{W}^{(\ell)}}\|^2, \end{equation} where $\matr{W}^{(\ell)}=(\matr{Y}\matr{X})^{{\blacklozenge}}\matr{A}^{(\ell)}(\matr{Y}\matr{X})\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the JADM cost over pairs (Y,X) in the Stiefel manifold times SL_m.

nodes.name: Cost function f(Y,X) on St x SL
nodes.statement: f: \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\times\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+},\ \ (\matr{Y},\matr{X})\mapsto \sum_{\ell=1}^{\matrelem{L}} \|\offdiag{\matr{W}^{(\ell)}}\|^2,
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem
nodes.label: eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi

nodes.name: Reduced matrices B^(l) for fixed Y_*
nodes.statement: Denote $\matr{B}^{(\ell)}=\matr{Y}_{*}^{{\blacklozenge}}\matr{A}^{(\ell)} \matr{Y}_{*}$ for $1\leq\ell\leq \matrelem{L}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem

nodes.name: JADM on SL_m(C) (second reformulation)
nodes.statement: Then the cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi} becomes \begin{equation} g: \mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+},\ \ \matr{X}\mapsto g(\matr{X})= \sum_{\ell=1}^{\matrelem{L}} \|\offdiag{\matr{W}^{(\ell)}}\|^2, \end{equation} where $\matr{W}^{(\ell)}=\matr{X}^{{\blacklozenge}}\matr{B}^{(\ell)} \matr{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem
nodes.statement_short: Minimize g(X)=sum of squared off-diagonal norms of X^♦ B^(l) X over SL_m.

nodes.name: Cost function g(X) on SL_m
nodes.statement: g: \mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+},\ \ \matr{X}\mapsto g(\matr{X})= \sum_{\ell=1}^{\matrelem{L}} \|\offdiag{\matr{W}^{(\ell)}}\|^2,
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem
nodes.label: eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-1

nodes.name: Square case reduces to SL_m
nodes.statement: Alternatively, this case may appear when $m=n$ in \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0}. Indeed, $\textbf{RSL}(m,m,\mathbb{C}) = \{\matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}, |\det(\matr{Z})| = 1\}$, and since \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0} is invariant with respect to multiplication by a unimodular scalar, we can optimize it over $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ instead.
nodes.section: 1.1 Search space and reformulations of the problem
nodes.statement_short: For m=n, RSL is the set of matrices with unimodular determinant, so one may optimize over SL_m.

nodes.name: Boundedness of BCD-G iterates
nodes.statement: Then their \emph{global convergence}\footnote{For any starting point, the iterates converge to a limit point as a whole sequence.} and \emph{weak convergence}\footnote{Every accumulation point is a stationary point, \emph{i.e.}, the Riemannian gradient is equal to 0.} will be established in \Cref{sec:BCD-G} using the \emph{\L{}ojasiewicz gradient inequality} \cite{loja1965ensembles,lojasiewicz1993geometrie,absil2005convergence,Usch15:pjo}, under the assumption that the iterates $\matr{\omega}_{k}$ are bounded, that is, there exists a universal positive constant $\mathrm{M}_{\omega}>0$ such that \begin{equation} \|\matr{\omega}_{k}\|\leq \mathrm{M}_{\omega} \end{equation} always holds for all $k\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: The BCD-G iterates ω_k are uniformly bounded by a constant M_ω.

nodes.name: Bound on iterates omega_k
nodes.statement: \|\matr{\omega}_{k}\|\leq \mathrm{M}_{\omega}
nodes.label: eq:condi_bounded_X_gene

nodes.name: Boundedness of Jacobi-G iterates
nodes.statement: Then their global and weak convergence will be established in \Cref{sec:BCD-G} using the \L{}ojasiewicz gradient inequality, under the assumption that the iterates $\matr{X}_{k}$ are bounded, that is, there exists a universal positive constant $\mathrm{M}_{\matr{X}}>0$ such that \begin{equation} \|\matr{X}_{k}\|\leq \mathrm{M}_{\matr{X}} \end{equation} always holds for all $k\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: The Jacobi-G iterates X_k are uniformly bounded by a constant M_X.

nodes.name: Bound on iterates X_k
nodes.statement: \|\matr{X}_{k}\|\leq \mathrm{M}_{\matr{X}}
nodes.label: eq:condi_bounded_X_gene-2

nodes.name: Block coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\{\mathcal{M}_i\}_{1\leq i\leq d}$ are smooth manifolds. To minimize a smooth function \begin{equation} \tilde{f}:\ \mathcal{M}_1\times\mathcal{M}_2\times\cdots\times\mathcal{M}_d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+}, \end{equation} a popular approach is the \emph{block coordinate descent} (BCD) algorithm \cite{bertsekas1997nonlinear,luo1992convergence,luo1993error,wright2015coordinate,xu2013block,li2019polar}. In this method, only one block variable is updated at each iteration, while other block variables are fixed; in other words, the problem \cref{definition-f-general} is decomposed into a sequence of lower-dimensional optimization problems.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize a function on a product of manifolds by updating one block variable at a time.
nodes.origin_citation: Bertsekas 1997; Luo & Tseng 1992; Wright 2015; Xu & Yin 2013

nodes.name: Smooth function on a product of manifolds
nodes.statement: \tilde{f}:\ \mathcal{M}_1\times\mathcal{M}_2\times\cdots\times\mathcal{M}_d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+},
nodes.label: definition-f-general

nodes.name: Restricted functions f_{1,X} and f_{2,Y}
nodes.statement: For $\matr{\omega}=(\matr{Y},\matr{X})\in\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\times\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$, we denote \begin{align} f_{1,\matr{X}}: \matr{Y}\mapsto f(\matr{Y},\matr{X}),\ \ f_{2,\matr{Y}}: \matr{X}\mapsto f(\matr{Y},\matr{X}), \end{align} as the two restricted functions, which are defined on $\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ and $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$, respectively.

nodes.name: Restricted functions
nodes.statement: f_{1,\matr{X}}: \matr{Y}\mapsto f(\matr{Y},\matr{X}),\ \ f_{2,\matr{Y}}: \matr{X}\mapsto f(\matr{Y},\matr{X}),
nodes.label: eq:restrc_functions

nodes.name: Block Riemannian gradients grad f_1, grad f_2
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we denote their \emph{Riemannian gradients}\footnote{See \cite[Section 3.6]{absil2009optimization} and \Cref{sec:geometr_basics} for a detailed definition.} as $\ProjGrad{f_{1}}{\matr{\omega}}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\ProjGrad{f_{1,\matr{X}}}{\matr{Y}}$ and $\ProjGrad{f_{2}}{\matr{\omega}}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\ProjGrad{f_{2,\matr{Y}}}{\matr{X}}$, and the Riemannian gradient of $f$ in \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi} at $\matr{\omega}$ as $\ProjGrad{f}{\matr{\omega}}$.

nodes.name: BCD-G algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{BCD-G algorithm} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE{{\bf Input:} A starting point $\matr{\omega}_{0}=(\matr{Y}_0,\matr{X}_0)$, a positive constant $0<\upsilon<\sqrt{2}/2$.} \STATE{{\bf Output:} Sequence of iterates $\matr{\omega}_{k}=(\matr{Y}_k,\matr{X}_k)$.} \FOR{$k=1,2,\cdots,$} \STATE Choose $t_k=1$ or $2$ such that the Riemannian gradients satisfy \begin{equation} \|\ProjGrad{f_{t_k}}{\matr{\omega}_{k-1}}\|\geq\upsilon\|\ProjGrad{f}{\matr{\omega}_{k-1}}\|; \end{equation} \vspace{-0.5cm} \IF {$t_k=1$} \STATE Update $\matr{Y}_{k}$ using the line search descent method (cf. \Cref{subsec:line_seach}); \STATE Set $\matr{X}_{k}=\matr{X}_{k-1}$; \ELSE \STATE Set $\matr{Y}_{k}=\matr{Y}_{k-1}$; \STATE Update $\matr{X}_{k}$ using elementary transformations (cf. \autoref{alg:jacobi-LU-G_c} to \ref{alg:jacob-GU-G_c}). \ENDIF \ENDFOR \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Block coordinate descent on St x SL choosing at each step a block whose Riemannian gradient is at least υ times the full gradient.
input: A starting point $\matr{\omega}_{0}=(\matr{Y}_0,\matr{X}_0)$, a positive constant $0<\upsilon<\sqrt{2}/2$.
nodes.label: alg:BCD-G-RL

nodes.name: Gradient-based block selection inequality
nodes.statement: \|\ProjGrad{f_{t_k}}{\matr{\omega}_{k-1}}\|\geq\upsilon\|\ProjGrad{f}{\matr{\omega}_{k-1}}\|;
nodes.label: eq:inequality_BCD_G

nodes.name: Proof that BCD-G is well defined (gradient splitting)
nodes.statement: Since the Riemannian gradients are related as \begin{align} \ProjGrad{f}{\matr{\omega}} = (\ProjGrad{f_1}{\matr{\omega}},\ \ProjGrad{f_2}{\matr{\omega}}), \end{align} we have that $\|\ProjGrad{f}{\matr{\omega}}\|^2=\|\ProjGrad{f_1}{\matr{\omega}}\|^2+\|\ProjGrad{f_2}{\matr{\omega}}\|^2.$
nodes.statement_short: The Riemannian gradient splits into the two block gradients, so their squared norms add up.

nodes.name: Splitting of the Riemannian gradient
nodes.statement: \ProjGrad{f}{\matr{\omega}} = (\ProjGrad{f_1}{\matr{\omega}},\ \ProjGrad{f_2}{\matr{\omega}}),
nodes.label: eq:grad_relation

nodes.name: BCD-G algorithm is well defined
nodes.statement: Therefore, in each iteration, if $0<\upsilon<\sqrt{2}/2$, we can always choose $t_k=1$ or $2$ such that the inequality \cref{eq:inequality_BCD_G} is satisfied, and thus \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL} is well defined.
conclusions: we can always choose $t_k=1$ or $2$ such that the inequality \cref{eq:inequality_BCD_G} is satisfied

nodes.name: Jacobi-G algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{Jacobi-G algorithm} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE{{\bf Input:} A starting point $\matr{X}_{0}$.} \STATE{{\bf Output:} Sequence of iterates $\{\matr{X}_{k}\}_{k\ge1}$.} \FOR{$k=1,2,\cdots,$} \STATE Update $\matr{X}_k$ using elementary transformations (cf. \autoref{alg:jacobi-LU-G_c} to \ref{alg:jacobi-LQ-G_c}). \ENDFOR \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Gradient-based Jacobi-type algorithm on SL_m updating X_k by elementary transformations.
nodes.label: alg:jacobi-LU-G_c-1

nodes.name: Jacobi-GLU and Jacobi-GQU algorithms
nodes.statement: As with BCD-G, two types of Jacobi-G exist: Jacobi-GLU and Jacobi-GQU, based on GLU and GQU classes of elementary transformations, respectively.

nodes.name: Upper triangular matrix
nodes.statement: A matrix $\matr{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$ is said to be \emph{upper triangular} if $\matrelem{X}_{ij}=0$ for $i>j$.

nodes.name: Upper triangular subgroup UT_m
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{UT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\subseteq\mathbf{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ be the \emph{upper triangular subgroup}.

nodes.name: EUT_m: upper triangular matrices of determinant 1
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbf{UT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\cap\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$, \emph{i.e.}, the set of upper triangular matrices with determinant equal to 1.

nodes.name: Lower triangular subgroup LT_m and ELT_m
nodes.statement: Similarly, we let $\mathbf{LT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$ be the \emph{lower triangular subgroup} and $\mathbf{ELT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})=\mathbf{LT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\cap\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$.

nodes.name: Unitary and special unitary groups
nodes.statement: Let $\UNN{m}(\mathbb{C})\subseteq \mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$ be the \emph{unitary group}, and $\SUNN{m}(\mathbb{C})\subseteq\UNN{m}(\mathbb{C})$ be the \emph{special unitary group}.

nodes.name: LU decomposition of SL_m
nodes.statement: Any matrix $\matr{X}\in\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ has the \emph{LU decomposition} \cite{GoluV96:jhu} $\matr{X}=\matr{L}\matr{U}$ with $\matr{L}\in\mathbf{LT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ and $\matr{U}\in\mathbf{UT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$.

nodes.name: Set product notation A • B
nodes.statement: We use the shorthand notation \begin{align} \mathbf{SL}_m(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbf{ELT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}), \end{align} where $\mathcal{A} \bullet \mathcal{B}$ denotes the set of all matrix product for matrices coming from two matrix sets $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$.

nodes.name: SL_m = ELT_m • EUT_m
nodes.statement: \mathbf{SL}_m(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbf{ELT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}),
nodes.label: eq:rela-equiavalent-5

nodes.name: QU decomposition of SL_m
nodes.statement: Any matrix $\matr{X}\in\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ has the \emph{QU decomposition}\footnote{This is also called QR decomposition in the literature.} $\matr{X}=\matr{Q}\matr{U}$ with $\matr{Q}\in\SUNN{m}(\mathbb{C})$ and $\matr{U}\in\mathbf{UT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$, which can be compactly written as \begin{align} \mathbf{SL}_m(\mathbb{C}) = \SUNN{m}(\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}). \end{align}

nodes.name: SL_m = SU_m • EUT_m
nodes.statement: \mathbf{SL}_m(\mathbb{C}) = \SUNN{m}(\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}).
nodes.label: eq:rela-equiavalent-6

nodes.name: LU- and QU-based decompositions of RSL
nodes.statement: Indeed, \Cref{lem:rela-equiavalent} in the compact notation can be written as \[ \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) =\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{SL}_m(\mathbb{C}), \] which gives rise to LU- and QU-based decompositions of $\textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$: \begin{align} \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) &= \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{ELT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}), \\ \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) &= \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\bullet\SUNN{m}(\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: RSL = St • SL, and hence RSL = St • ELT • EUT and RSL = St • SU • EUT.

nodes.name: RSL = St • ELT • EUT
nodes.statement: \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) &= \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{ELT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}),
nodes.label: eq:rela-equiavalent-2

nodes.name: RSL = St • SU • EUT
nodes.statement: \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) &= \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\bullet\SUNN{m}(\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}).
nodes.label: eq:rela-equiavalent-3

nodes.name: Third decomposition RSL = St • EUT
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $\textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$, a third decomposition is possible, using the fact that $\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\bullet\SUNN{m}(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$. Then the equation \cref{eq:rela-equiavalent-3} can be simplified as \begin{align} \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) =\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}), \end{align} which can also be interpreted as applying the QU decomposition to a rectangular matrix from $\textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$.

nodes.name: RSL = St • EUT
nodes.statement: \textbf{RSL}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) =\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})\bullet\mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}),
nodes.label: eq:rela-equiavalent-13

nodes.name: Unipotent upper triangular matrix
nodes.statement: An upper triangular matrix $\matr{X}$ is said to be \emph{unipotent} if it satisfies $\matrelem{X}_{ii}=1$ for $1\leq i\leq m$.

nodes.name: Upper unipotent subgroup SUT_m
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{SUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\subseteq \mathbf{EUT}_{m}(\mathbb{C}) $ be the \emph{upper unipotent subgroup} of unipotent upper triangular matrices.

nodes.name: Lower unipotent subgroup SLT_m
nodes.statement: Similarly, we let $\mathbf{SLT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\subseteq \mathbf{ELT}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ be the \emph{lower unipotent subgroup}.

nodes.name: Diagonal transformation
nodes.statement: Finally, a diagonal matrix $\matr{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$ is said to be a \emph{diagonal transformation} if the product of all the diagonal elements is equal to 1.
differentia: the product of all the diagonal elements is equal to 1

nodes.name: Set D_m of diagonal transformations
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{D}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\subseteq\mathbf{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ be the set of diagonal transformation matrices.

nodes.name: 2x2 groups SUT_2, SLT_2, D_2
nodes.statement: The elementary transformations are based on the following $2\times 2$ matrices: {\small \begin{align*} \mathbf{SUT}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) = \left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & z\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}, z\in\mathbb{C}\right\},\ \mathbf{SLT}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) = \left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ z& 1 \end{bmatrix}, z\in\mathbb{C}\right\},\ \mathbf{D}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) = \left\{\begin{bmatrix} z & 0\\ 0& \frac{1}{z} \end{bmatrix}, z\in\mathbb{C}_{*}\right\}, \end{align*}} as well as the $2\times 2$ matrices from $\SUNN{2}(\mathbb{C})$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit 2x2 unipotent upper, unipotent lower and determinant-one diagonal matrix groups.

nodes.name: Embedding operator E_{i,j}
nodes.statement: We introduce an operator $\mathcal{E}_{i,j}: \mathbb{C}^{2\times 2} \to\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$ sending $\Psi$ to $\matr{X} \in \mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$ satisfying \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} \matrelem{X}_{ii} & \matrelem{X}_{ij}\\ \matrelem{X}_{ji}& \matrelem{X}_{jj} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \matrelem{\Psi}_{11} & \matrelem{\Psi}_{12}\\ \matrelem{\Psi}_{21}& \matrelem{\Psi}_{22} \end{bmatrix}, \ \ \bigg\{ \begin{aligned} \matrelem{X}_{\ell\ell} = 1,\ \ & \text{if}\ \ell \not\in \{i,j\}, \\ \matrelem{X}_{k\ell} = 0,\ \ & \text{otherwise}. \end{aligned} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: E_{i,j} embeds a 2x2 matrix into the (i,j) rows/columns of the m x m identity.

nodes.name: Four elementary transformations (Givens, upper/lower triangular, diagonal)
nodes.statement: Now we define the following four elementary transformations on $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$: \begin{itemize} \item $\Gmat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\mathcal{E}_{i,j}(\matr{\Psi})$: \emph{Givens plane transformation} for $\matr{\Psi} \in \SUNN{2}(\mathbb{C})$; \item $\Umat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\mathcal{E}_{i,j}(\matr{\Psi})$: \emph{plane upper triangular transformation} for $\matr{\Psi} \in \mathbf{SUT}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$; \item $\Lmat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\mathcal{E}_{i,j}(\matr{\Psi})$: \emph{plane lower triangular transformation} for $\matr{\Psi} \in \mathbf{SLT}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$; \item $\Dmat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\mathcal{E}_{i,j}(\matr{\Psi})$: \emph{plane diagonal transformation} for $\matr{\Psi} \in \mathbf{D}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Givens, plane upper/lower triangular and plane diagonal transformations are E_{i,j} applied to SU_2, SUT_2, SLT_2, D_2.

nodes.name: Elementary transformations in the literature
nodes.statement: These elementary transformations have all been used in the literature. The Givens transformations $\Gmat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}}$ were used very often in the Jacobi-type algorithms for joint approximate diagonalization of matrices or tensors by orthogonal or non-orthogonal transformations \cite{Como10:book,LUC2017globally,ULC2019,Afsa07:honolulu,afsari2006simple,sorensen2009approximate}. Triangular transformations $\Umat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}}$ and $\Lmat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}}$ also appeared many times in the Jacobi-type algorithms on $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ or $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{R})$ \cite{afsari2004gradient,afsari2006simple,maurandi2013fast,maurandi2014decoupled,maurandi2014jacobi}. In the real case, the diagonal transformation $\Dmat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}}$ was once used in \cite{souloumiac2009nonorthogonal}.
nodes.statement_short: Givens, triangular and diagonal transformations have all been used in prior Jacobi-type algorithms.

nodes.name: GLU, GQU and GU classes of elementary transformations
nodes.statement: The iterates $\matr{X}_k$ in \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL} and \Cref{alg:jacobi-LU-G_c-1} are updated multiplicatively as $\matr{X}_k = \matr{X}_{k-1}\matr{P}_{k}$, where $\matr{P}_{k}$ is an elementary transformation for a pair of indices $(i_k,j_k)$ belonging to one of the following three classes. These three classes are inspired by equations \cref{eq:rela-equiavalent-2}, \cref{eq:rela-equiavalent-3}, \cref{eq:rela-equiavalent-13} and by a similar idea as in \cite{IshtAV13:simax,LUC2017globally,ULC2019}. We call them the \emph{GLU} (based on LU decomposition), \emph{GQU} (based on QU decomposition) and GU transformations, respectively. \begin{itemize} \item {GLU class}: $\matr{P}_{k}=\Lmat{i_k}{j_k}{\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}},\ \Umat{i_k}{j_k}{\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}}$ or $\Dmat{i_k}{j_k}{\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}}$; \item GQU class: $\matr{P}_{k}=\Gmat{i_k}{j_k}{\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}},\ \Umat{i_k}{j_k}{\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}}$ or $\Dmat{i_k}{j_k}{\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}}$; \item GU class: $\matr{P}_{k}= \Umat{i_k}{j_k}{\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}}$ or $\Dmat{i_k}{j_k}{\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: X_k = X_{k-1} P_k with P_k from the GLU (L,U,D), GQU (G,U,D) or GU (U,D) class of elementary transformations.

nodes.name: Validity in the real case
nodes.statement: While the algorithms and convergence results described in this paper are provided for complex matrices, complex Stiefel manifold $\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ and complex special linear group $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$, they also remain valid in the real case.

nodes.name: Real and imaginary parts notation
nodes.statement: For a complex matrix $\matr{Z}\in \mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$ and a complex number $z\in \mathbb{C}$, we write the real and imaginary parts as $\matr{Z} =\matr{Z}^{\Re} + i \matr{Z}^{\Im}$ and $z=\Re(z)+i\Im(z)$, respectively.

nodes.name: Real-valued inner product on C^{n x m}
nodes.statement: For complex matrices $\matr{Z}_1,\matr{Z}_2\in \mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$, we introduce the following real-valued inner product \begin{equation} \RInner{\matr{Z}_1}{\matr{Z}_2} \stackrel{\sf def}{=} \langle\matr{Z}_1^{\Re},\matr{Z}_2^{\Re} \rangle + \langle\matr{Z}_1^{\Im},\matr{Z}_2^{\Im} \rangle = \Re \left({\trace{\matr{Z}_1^{{\sf H}}\matr{Z}_2}}\right), \end{equation} which makes $\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$ a real Euclidean space of dimension $2nm$.

nodes.name: Real inner product
nodes.statement: \RInner{\matr{Z}_1}{\matr{Z}_2} \stackrel{\sf def}{=} \langle\matr{Z}_1^{\Re},\matr{Z}_2^{\Re} \rangle + \langle\matr{Z}_1^{\Im},\matr{Z}_2^{\Im} \rangle = \Re \left({\trace{\matr{Z}_1^{{\sf H}}\matr{Z}_2}}\right),
nodes.label: eq:RInner

nodes.name: Matrix Euclidean derivatives w.r.t. real and imaginary parts
nodes.statement: Let $h:\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function and $\matr{Z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$. We denote by $\frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Re},\frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Im} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ the matrix Euclidean derivatives of $h$ with respect to real and imaginary parts of $\matr{Z}$.

nodes.name: Wirtinger derivatives
nodes.statement: The \emph{Wirtinger derivatives} \cite{abrudan2008steepest,brandwood1983complex,krantz2001function} are defined as \begin{equation*} \frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^{*}} \stackrel{\sf def}{=} \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Re}+ i\frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Im}\right), \quad \frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}} \stackrel{\sf def}{=} \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Re}- i\frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Im}\right). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Euclidean gradient of a real function of a complex matrix
nodes.statement: Then the Euclidean gradient of $h$ with respect to the inner product \cref{eq:RInner} becomes \begin{equation} \nabla h(\matr{Z}) = \frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Re}+ i\frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Im} = 2 \frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^{*}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Euclidean gradient via Wirtinger derivative
nodes.statement: \nabla h(\matr{Z}) = \frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Re}+ i\frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^\Im} = 2 \frac{\partial h}{\partial\matr{Z}^{*}}.
nodes.label: eq:matr_Euci_grad

nodes.name: Unit sphere S_2 and C_*
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathbb{S}_{2}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3}$ the unit sphere, and $\mathbb{C}_{*}=\mathbb{C}\backslash \{0\}$.

nodes.name: Hermitian and skew-Hermitian parts sym(C), skew(C)
nodes.statement: For a matrix $\matr{C}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}$, we denote $\symmm{\matr{C}}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\frac{1}{2}(\matr{C}+\matr{C}^{{\sf H}})$ and $\skeww{\matr{C}}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\frac{1}{2}(\matr{C}-\matr{C}^{{\sf H}})$.

nodes.name: Tangent space to the Stiefel manifold
nodes.statement: Let ${\rm\bf T}_{\matr{Y}} \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ be the \emph{tangent space} to $\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$ at a point $\matr{Y}\in\mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})$.

nodes.name: Orthogonal complement Y_perp
nodes.statement: Let $\matr{Y}_{\perp}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times (n-m)}$ be an orthogonal complement of $\matr{Y}$, that is, $[\matr{Y}, \matr{Y}_{\perp}]\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ is a unitary matrix.

nodes.name: Tangent space to St(m,n,C)
nodes.statement: {\small {\rm\bf T}_{\matr{Y}} \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C}) = \{\matr{V}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}, \matr{V}=\matr{Y}\matr{C}+\matr{Y}_{\perp}\matr{B}, \matr{C}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}, \matr{C}^{{\sf H}}+\matr{C}=0, \matr{B}\in\mathbb{C}^{(n-m)\times m}\},}
nodes.label: eq:tanget_spac

nodes.name: Orthogonal projection onto the Stiefel tangent space
nodes.statement: {\rm Proj}_{\matr{Y}} \xi = (\matr{I}_{n}-\matr{Y}\matr{Y}^{{\sf H}})\xi + \matr{Y}\skeww{\matr{Y}^{{\sf H}}\xi} =\xi - \matr{Y}\symmm{\matr{Y}^{{\sf H}}\xi}.
nodes.label: eq:proj_Stiefel

nodes.name: Riemannian gradient on the Stiefel manifold
nodes.label: eq:Rie_grad

nodes.name: Exponential map on the Stiefel manifold
nodes.statement: By \cite[Example 5.4.2]{absil2009optimization}, the \emph{exponential map} at $\matr{Y}$ is defined as \begin{align}{\small {\rm Exp}_{\matr{Y}}: {\rm\bf T}_{\matr{Y}} \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})}&{\small\longrightarrow \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})}\\ {\small\matr{V}}&{\small\longmapsto [\matr{Y}, \matr{V}] \expp{ \begin{bmatrix} \matr{Y}^{H}\matr{V} &-\matr{V}^{{\sf H}}\matr{V}\\ \matr{I}_{m} &\matr{Y}^{H}\matr{V} \end{bmatrix}} \begin{bmatrix} \expp{-\matr{Y}^{H}\matr{V}} \\ \matr{0}_{m\times m} \end{bmatrix},\notag} \end{align} where $\exp(\cdot)$ is the matrix exponential function \cite{absil2009optimization,baker2012matrix,Hall15:lie}.

nodes.name: Stiefel exponential map formula
nodes.statement: {\small {\rm Exp}_{\matr{Y}}: {\rm\bf T}_{\matr{Y}} \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})}&{\small\longrightarrow \mathbf{St}(m,n,\mathbb{C})}\\ {\small\matr{V}}&{\small\longmapsto [\matr{Y}, \matr{V}] \expp{ \begin{bmatrix} \matr{Y}^{H}\matr{V} &-\matr{V}^{{\sf H}}\matr{V}\\ \matr{I}_{m} &\matr{Y}^{H}\matr{V} \end{bmatrix}} \begin{bmatrix} \expp{-\matr{Y}^{H}\matr{V}} \\ \matr{0}_{m\times m} \end{bmatrix},\notag}
nodes.label: eq:ex_sl_pr

nodes.name: Lie algebra sl_m(C)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{sl}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\{\matr{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}, \mbox{tr}(\matr{X})=0\}$ be the \emph{Lie algebra} \cite{baker2012matrix} of the complex special linear group $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$.

nodes.name: Tangent space to SL_m
nodes.statement: \mathbf{T}_{\matr{X}}\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}) = \{\matr{X}\Omega, \Omega\in\mathfrak{sl}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\}.
nodes.label: eq:tang_slm

nodes.name: Lie algebra su_m(C)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{su}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\{\matr{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times m}, \matr{X}^{{\sf H}} = -\matr{X}, \mbox{tr}(\matr{X})=0\}$ be the Lie algebra of the special unitary group $\SUNN{m}(\mathbb{C})$.

nodes.name: Left invariant Riemannian metric on SL_m
nodes.statement: For tangent matrices $\matr{V}_1, \matr{V}_2\in\mathbf{T}_{\matr{X}}\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$, we use the \emph{left invariant} \cite{absil2009optimization}, \cite[Eq. (6.2)]{afsari2004gradient} Riemannian metric \begin{equation*} \langle\matr{V}_1, \matr{V}_2\rangle_{\matr{X}} \stackrel{\sf def}{=} \RInner{\matr{X}^{-1}\matr{V}_1}{\matr{X}^{-1}\matr{V}_2} = \Re \left({\trace{\matr{V}_1^{{\sf H}}(\matr{X}\matr{X}^{{\sf H}})^{-1}\matr{V}_2}}\right). \end{equation*}
nodes.origin_citation: Absil et al. 2008; Afsari & Krishnaprasad 2004, Eq. (6.2)

nodes.name: Riemannian gradient on SL_m
nodes.statement: \ProjGrad{g}{\matr{X}} = \matr{X}\left(\matr{X}^{{\sf H}}\nabla g(\matr{X}) - \frac{\mbox{tr}(\matr{X}^{{\sf H}}\nabla g(\matr{X}))}{n}\matr{I}_n\right).
nodes.label: eq:riema_gradient_c

nodes.name: Lambda(X) = X^{-1} grad g(X)
nodes.statement: We denote $\matr{\Lambda}(\matr{X})\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\matr{X}^{-1}\ProjGrad{g}{\matr{X}}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ for $\matr{X}\in\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$, which will be frequently used in this paper.

nodes.name: Exponential map on SL_m
nodes.statement: In what follows, we will use the following exponential map \begin{equation} \text{Exp}_{\matr{X}}: \mathbf{T}_{\matr{X}}\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}) \to \mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}),\ \ \matr{X}\Omega\mapsto\matr{X} \exp(\Omega), \end{equation} where $\exp(\cdot)$ is the matrix exponential function \cite{absil2009optimization,baker2012matrix,Hall15:lie}.

nodes.name: Exponential map on SL_m
nodes.statement: \text{Exp}_{\matr{X}}: \mathbf{T}_{\matr{X}}\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}) \to \mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}),\ \ \matr{X}\Omega\mapsto\matr{X} \exp(\Omega),
nodes.label: eq:Exp_x_sl

nodes.name: Gradient / exponential map relation

nodes.name: Łojasiewicz gradient inequality
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{M} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a Riemannian submanifold, and $\varphi: \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function. The function $\varphi: \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}$ is said to satisfy a \emph{\L{}ojasiewicz gradient inequality} at $\vect{x} \in \mathcal{M}$, if there exist $\delta>0$, $\zeta\in (0,\frac{1}{2}]$ and a neighborhood $\mathcal{U}$ in $\mathcal{M}$ of $\vect{x}$ such that for all $\vect{y}\in\mathcal{U}$, it follows that \begin{equation} |{\varphi}(\vect{y})-{\varphi}(\vect{x})|^{1-\zeta}\leq \delta\|\ProjGrad{\varphi}{\vect{y}}\|. \end{equation}
nodes.label: def:Lojasiewicz

nodes.name: Łojasiewicz inequality
nodes.statement: |{\varphi}(\vect{y})-{\varphi}(\vect{x})|^{1-\zeta}\leq \delta\|\ProjGrad{\varphi}{\vect{y}}\|.
nodes.label: eq:Lojasiewicz

nodes.name: Analytic functions satisfy the Łojasiewicz inequality

Then $\varphi$ satisfies a \L{}ojasiewicz gradient inequality \cref{eq:Lojasiewicz} at any $\vect{x}\in \mathcal{M}$.
conclusions: $\varphi$ satisfies a \L{}ojasiewicz gradient inequality \cref{eq:Lojasiewicz} at any $\vect{x}\in \mathcal{M}$
nodes.label: lemma-SU15

nodes.name: Schneider–Uschmajew convergence theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ be an analytic submanifold and $\{\vect{x}_k\}_{k\geq 1}\subseteq\mathcal{M}$. Suppose that $\varphi$ is real analytic and, for large enough $k$,\\ (i) there exists $\sigma>0$ such that \begin{equation*} \varphi(\vect{x}_{k})-{\varphi}(\vect{x}_{k+1})\geq \sigma\|\ProjGrad{\varphi}{\vect{x}_k}\|\|\vect{x}_{k+1}-\vect{x}_{k}\|; \end{equation*} (ii) $\ProjGrad{\varphi}{\vect{x}_k}=0$ implies that $\vect{x}_{k+1}=\vect{x}_{k}$.\\ Then, if $\vect{x}_*$ is an accumulation point of $\{\vect{x}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$, it is the limit point.
conclusions: if $\vect{x}_*$ is an accumulation point of $\{\vect{x}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$, it is the limit point
nodes.statement_short: Sufficient descent plus a stationarity-safeguard imply that any accumulation point of the iterates is their limit.
nodes.label: theorem-SU15

nodes.name: Justification of the BCD-G global convergence lemma
nodes.statement: However, if there exists an accumulation point, we have the following result about its global convergence, which is a direct consequence of \Cref{theorem-SU15} and inequality \cref{eq:inequality_BCD_G}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of the Schneider–Uschmajew theorem combined with the block selection inequality.

nodes.name: Global convergence criterion for BCD-G
nodes.statement: Suppose that, in \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL} for cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}, the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ satisfy that, for large enough $k$,\\ (i) there exists $\sigma>0$ such that \begin{equation} f(\matr{\omega}_{k-1})-f(\matr{\omega}_{k})\geq\sigma\|\ProjGrad{f_{t_k}}{\matr{\omega}_{k-1}}\|\|\matr{\omega}_{k}-\matr{\omega}_{k-1}\|; \end{equation} (ii) $\ProjGrad{f_{t_k}}{\matr{\omega}_{k-1}}=0$ implies that $\matr{\omega}_{k}=\matr{\omega}_{k-1}$.\\ Then, if $\matr{\omega}_*$ is an accumulation point of the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$, it is the limit point.
conclusions: if $\matr{\omega}_*$ is an accumulation point of the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$, it is the limit point

In particular, if $\matr{\omega}_*$ is an accumulation point of the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_{k}\}_{k\ge1}$, then $\matr{\omega}_*$ is a stationary point of $f$.

if $\matr{\omega}_*$ is an accumulation point of the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_{k}\}_{k\ge1}$,

nodes.name: Unit vector r(theta,phi)
nodes.statement: As in \cite[Eq. (4.4)]{ULC2019}, we denote the unit vector \begin{align} \vect{r} \stackrel{\sf def}{=}\left[2c^2-1,\ -2cs_1,\ -2cs_2\right]^{{\sf T}} = \left[\cos 2\theta,\ -\sin 2\theta\cos\phi,\ -\sin 2\theta\sin\phi\right]^{{\sf T}}, \end{align} where $c\in \mathbb{R}^{+}$, $s= s_1 + i s_2\in\mathbb{C}$, $c^2+|s|^2 =1$, and $\theta,\phi\in\mathbb{R}$ are two angles.

nodes.name: Definition of r
nodes.statement: \vect{r} \stackrel{\sf def}{=}\left[2c^2-1,\ -2cs_1,\ -2cs_2\right]^{{\sf T}} = \left[\cos 2\theta,\ -\sin 2\theta\cos\phi,\ -\sin 2\theta\sin\phi\right]^{{\sf T}},

nodes.name: Justification of the Givens elementary function expression
nodes.statement: Then we can get the following result\footnote{In the $(\cdot)^{{\blacklozenge}}=(\cdot)^{{\sf H}}$ case, this expression was first formulated in \cite{cardoso1996jacobi}.} by direct calculations.
nodes.statement_short: Direct calculation.

nodes.name: Quadratic-form expression of the Givens elementary function
nodes.statement: In \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL} for cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}, the elementary function $h^{(Q)}_k$ satisfies \begin{align} h^{(Q)}_k(c,s_1,s_2) - h^{(Q)}_k(1,0,0) = -\left(\vect{r}^{{\sf T}}\Gamij{i}{j}{\matr{X}_{k-1}}\vect{r} - c_0\right), \end{align} where $\Gamij{i}{j}{\matr{X}_{k-1}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ is as in equation \cref{eq:gamma_matr_ij}.
nodes.statement_short: The Givens elementary function decrease is minus a quadratic form r^T Γ r shifted by c_0.
nodes.label: lemm:elemen_express_c_1

nodes.name: h^(Q) via Gamma
nodes.statement: h^{(Q)}_k(c,s_1,s_2) - h^{(Q)}_k(1,0,0) = -\left(\vect{r}^{{\sf T}}\Gamij{i}{j}{\matr{X}_{k-1}}\vect{r} - c_0\right),
nodes.label: eq:elemen_h_Gamma

nodes.name: Expression of h^(Q)_k via q(theta,phi)
nodes.statement: It follows by equations \cref{eq:w_definition} and \cref{eq:elemen_h_Gamma} that \begin{align} h^{(Q)}_k(c,s_1,s_2) - h^{(Q)}_k(1,0,0) &= -\left(q(\theta,\phi)-c_0\right), \end{align} where {\small \begin{align} q(\theta,\phi)&\stackrel{\sf def}{=} \frac{1}{2}\left(\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22}\cos^2\phi-\Gamma_{33}\sin^2\phi-\Gamma_{23}\sin(2\phi)\right)\cos(4\theta)\notag\\ &\quad-\left(\Gamma_{12}\cos\phi+\Gamma_{13}\sin\phi\right)\sin(4\theta) +\frac{1}{2}\left(\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22}\cos^2\phi+\Gamma_{33}\sin^2\phi+\Gamma_{23}\sin(2\phi)\right). \end{align}}
nodes.statement_short: In angle coordinates the Givens elementary function equals −(q(θ,φ) − c_0) with q a trigonometric polynomial in 4θ.

nodes.name: Definition of q(theta,phi)
nodes.statement: q(\theta,\phi)&\stackrel{\sf def}{=} \frac{1}{2}\left(\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22}\cos^2\phi-\Gamma_{33}\sin^2\phi-\Gamma_{23}\sin(2\phi)\right)\cos(4\theta)\notag\\ &\quad-\left(\Gamma_{12}\cos\phi+\Gamma_{13}\sin\phi\right)\sin(4\theta) +\frac{1}{2}\left(\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22}\cos^2\phi+\Gamma_{33}\sin^2\phi+\Gamma_{23}\sin(2\phi)\right).
nodes.label: eq:q_tehta

nodes.name: Partial derivative of h^(Q) at I_2
nodes.statement: \partial h^{(Q)}_k(\matr{I}_2) =-4 [0,\ \Gamma_{12},\ \Gamma_{13}]^{\sf T}.
nodes.label: eq:partial_h_k

nodes.name: Periodicity of h^(Q) in theta
nodes.statement: By equation \cref{eq:h_k_theta}, we see that $h^{(Q)}_k(\theta+\pi/{2},\phi)=h^{(Q)}_k(\theta,\phi)$ for any $\theta,\phi\in\mathbb{R}$. Therefore, we can always choose $\theta_{*}\in[-\pi/{4},\pi/{4}]$.

nodes.name: Update rule 3 (Givens transformations)
nodes.statement: In \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL} for cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}, we set a positive constant $\varsigma_{Q}>0$. If $h_k=h^{(Q)}_k$, we find the eigenvector $\vect{u}$ of $\matr{\Gamma}$ corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. Define two vectors $\vect{v}_{i,j}\stackrel{\sf def}{=}\left[\Gamma_{12},\ \Gamma_{13}\right]^{\sf T}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\vect{w}_{i,j}\stackrel{\sf def}{=} \left[u_2,\ u_3\right]^{\sf T}\in\mathbb{R}^2.$ \begin{itemize} \item If it holds that \begin{equation} |\langle\vect{v}_{i,j},\vect{w}_{i,j}\rangle| \geq\varsigma_{Q}\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\|\|\vect{w}_{i,j}\|, \end{equation} then we find $\phi_*$ and $\theta_*$ by setting $\vect{r}=\vect{u}$, and $\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}=\matr{\Psi}(\theta_*,\phi_*)$; \item Otherwise, we set $[\cos\phi_*,\ \sin\phi_*]^{\sf T}=\vect{v}_{i,j}/{\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\|}$, and then calculate $\theta_*$, which maximizes the restricted function $q(\theta,\phi_{*})$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Choose (θ*,φ*) from the top eigenvector of Γ if it is well aligned with v_{i,j}, otherwise fix φ* along v_{i,j} and maximize q over θ.
nodes.label: remark:condition_inner

nodes.name: Alignment condition
nodes.statement: |\langle\vect{v}_{i,j},\vect{w}_{i,j}\rangle| \geq\varsigma_{Q}\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\|\|\vect{w}_{i,j}\|,
nodes.label: eq:condition_phi_1

nodes.name: Lower bound for the maximum of a cos(4θ)+b sin(4θ)
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ be two constants. For $\theta\in[-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}]$, we define a function $p(\theta)\stackrel{\sf def}{=} \alpha\cos(4\theta) + \beta\sin(4\theta)$. If $\theta_{*}\in[-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}]$ satisfies $p(\theta_{*})=\max p(\theta)$, then we have \begin{equation*} p(\theta_{*})-p(0)\geq 2\sqrt{2}|\beta|\left|\sin(\frac{\theta_*}{2})\right|. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lemm:g-theta

nodes.name: Increase of q at the chosen angles
nodes.statement: Let the function $q(\theta,\phi)$ be as in equation \cref{eq:q_tehta}. Suppose that $\phi_*$ and $\theta_*$ are determined as in \Cref{remark:condition_inner}. Then we have \begin{equation*} q(\theta_*,\phi_*)-q(0,0)\geq 2\sqrt{2}\varsigma_{Q} \left|\sin(\frac{\theta_{*}}{2})\right|\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\|, \end{equation*} where $\varsigma_{Q}$ is the positive constant defined in \Cref{remark:condition_inner}.
assumptions: the function $q(\theta,\phi)$ be as in equation \cref{eq:q_tehta}
nodes.label: lem:p_theta_phi

nodes.name: Proof of the increase of q
nodes.statement: By \Cref{remark:condition_inner}, we see that \begin{equation} |\langle\vect{v}_{i,j},[\cos\phi_*\ \sin\phi_*]^{\sf T}\rangle| \geq\varsigma_{Q}\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\| \end{equation} always holds. By \Cref{lemm:g-theta} and the above inequality \cref{eq:condition_phi_2}, we get that \begin{align*} q(\theta_{*},\phi_{*})-q(0,0)&=q(\theta_{*},\phi_{*})-q(0,\phi_{*})\geq 2\sqrt{2}\left|\sin(\frac{\theta_*}{2})\right||\Gamma_{12}\cos\phi_*+\Gamma_{13}\sin\phi_*|\\ &\geq 2\sqrt{2} \varsigma_{Q}\left|\sin(\frac{\theta_*}{2})\right|\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\|. \end{align*} The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: The update rule guarantees alignment of φ* with v_{i,j}; then apply the bound for a cos 4θ + b sin 4θ.

nodes.name: Alignment of phi_* with v_{i,j}
nodes.statement: |\langle\vect{v}_{i,j},[\cos\phi_*\ \sin\phi_*]^{\sf T}\rangle| \geq\varsigma_{Q}\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\|
nodes.label: eq:condition_phi_2

nodes.name: Descent inequality for the Givens transformation
nodes.statement: In \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL} for cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}, there exists $\iota_{Q}>0$ such that \begin{equation} g(\matr{X}_{k-1})-g(\matr{X}_{k})\geq\iota_{Q}\|\matr{\Lambda}(\matr{X}_{k-1})\|\|\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}-\matr{I}_{2}\|, \end{equation} whenever the elementary function $h_k=h^{(Q)}_{k}$.

nodes.statement: g(\matr{X}_{k-1})-g(\matr{X}_{k})\geq\iota_{Q}\|\matr{\Lambda}(\matr{X}_{k-1})\|\|\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}-\matr{I}_{2}\|,

nodes.name: Proof of the Givens descent inequality
nodes.statement: We only prove the case $(\cdot)^{{\blacklozenge}}=(\cdot)^{{\sf H}}$, the other case being similar. By \Cref{lem:p_theta_phi} and equation \cref{eq:partial_h_k}, we get that \begin{align*} h^{(Q)}_k(0,0)-h^{(Q)}_k(\theta_*,\phi_*) &\geq 2\sqrt{2}\varsigma_{Q} \left|\sin(\frac{\theta_{*}}{2})\right|\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\| = \frac{\varsigma_{Q}}{4} 2\sqrt{2}\left|\sin(\frac{\theta_{*}}{2})\right|\|\partial h^{(Q)}_k(\matr{I}_2)\|\\ &\geq \frac{\varsigma_{Q}\varepsilon}{4} \|\Gmat{i}{j}{\matr{\Psi}_{k}^{*}}-\matr{I}_m\|\|\matr{\Lambda}(\matr{X}_{k-1})\|. \end{align*} We can set $\iota_{Q}=(\varsigma_{Q}\varepsilon)/{4}$. The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the increase of q with the partial derivative formula and the selection inequality.

nodes.name: sigma_Q
nodes.statement: Let $\iota_{Q}$ be as in \cref{equation-condition-weak_c-5-1} and $\mathrm{M}_{\omega}$ be as in condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene}. Let $\sigma_{Q}=\iota_{Q}/\mathrm{M}_{\omega}^2>0$.

nodes.name: Justification of the Givens sufficient descent corollary
nodes.statement: As for \Cref{lemma:global_rho_c}, the next result follows directly from \Cref{lemma:h_k_condition_SU-0}, inequalities \cref{eq:x_k_x_k-1_1} and \cref{eq:x_k_x_k-1_2}.

nodes.statement: In \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL} for cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}, if the iterates remain bounded, i.e., the condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene} is satisfied, then \begin{equation*} g(\matr{X}_{k-1})-g(\matr{X}_{k})\geq\sigma_{Q}\|\ProjGrad{g}{\matr{X}_{k-1}}\|\|\matr{X}_{k}-\matr{X}_{k-1}\|, \end{equation*} whenever the elementary function $h_k=h^{(Q)}_{k}$.

nodes.name: Boundedness of Gamma_{i,j}
nodes.statement: If the condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene} is satisfied, it is easy to see that there exists a positive constant $\mathrm{M}_{\Gamma}>0$ such that $\|\Gamij{i}{j}{\matr{X}_{k-1}}\|\leq \mathrm{M}_{\Gamma}$ always holds in \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL}.
conclusions: there exists a positive constant  $\mathrm{M}_{\Gamma}>0$ such that $\|\Gamij{i}{j}{\matr{X}_{k-1}}\|\leq \mathrm{M}_{\Gamma}$ always holds in \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL}

nodes.statement: In \Cref{alg:BCD-G-RL} for cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}, if the iterates remain bounded, i.e., the condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene} is satisfied, then there exists $\kappa_{Q}>0$ such that \begin{equation} \|\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}-\matr{I}_{2}\|\geq \kappa_{Q}\|\matr{\Lambda}(\matr{X}_{k-1})\|, \end{equation} whenever the elementary function $h_k=h^{(Q)}_{k}$.
assumptions: the iterates remain bounded, i.e., the condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene} is satisfied

nodes.name: Step size lower bound (Q case)
nodes.statement: \|\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}-\matr{I}_{2}\|\geq \kappa_{Q}\|\matr{\Lambda}(\matr{X}_{k-1})\|,

nodes.name: Proof of the Givens step size lower bound
nodes.statement: If $\vect{v}_{i,j}$ and $\vect{w}_{i,j}$ satisfy inequality \cref{eq:condition_phi_1}, then inequality \cref{equation-condition-weak_c-4-3} can be proved by a similar method as for \cite[Lemma 7.2]{ULC2019}. Otherwise, if we set $[\cos\phi_*\ \sin\phi_*]^{\sf T}=\vect{v}_{i,j}/{\|\vect{v}_{i,j}\|}$ and find $\theta_*$ based on $\phi_*$, then \begin{align*} |\sin(4\theta_{*})|&=\frac{\left|\Gamma_{12}\cos\phi_*+\Gamma_{13}\sin\phi_*\right|}{\sqrt{\left(\Gamma_{12}\cos\phi_*+\Gamma_{13}\sin\phi_*\right)^2+\frac{1}{4}\left(\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22}\cos^2\phi_*-\Gamma_{33}\sin^2\phi_*-\Gamma_{23}\sin(2\phi_*)\right)^2}}\\ &\geq \frac{\sqrt{\Gamma_{12}^2+\Gamma_{13}^2}}{2\sqrt{5}\mathrm{M}_{\Gamma}} =\frac{\|\partial h^{(Q)}_k(\matr{I}_2)\|}{8\sqrt{5}\mathrm{M}_{\Gamma}} \geq \frac{\varepsilon}{8\sqrt{5}\mathrm{M}_{\Gamma}}\|\matr{\Lambda}(\matr{X}_{k-1})\|. \end{align*} Note that \begin{align*} \|\matr{\Psi}^{*}_{k}-\matr{I}_{2}\| = 2\sqrt{2}\left|\sin(\frac{\theta_{*}}{2})\right| \geq \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}|\sin(4\theta_{*})|. \end{align*} We only need to set $\kappa_{Q}=\frac{\sqrt{2}\varepsilon}{32\sqrt{5}\mathrm{M}_{\Gamma}}$ in this case. The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on the alignment condition: cite the unitary-group argument, or bound |sin 4θ*| below via the gradient and M_Γ.

nodes.name: Justification of the Givens squared-gradient descent corollary
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lemma:h_k_condition_SU-0}, \Cref{lemma:weak_rho_inequality_c-3}, inequalities \cref{eq:x_k_x_k-1_1} and \cref{eq:x_k_x_k-1_2}, we can now easily get the following result by setting $\eta_{Q}=(\kappa_{Q}\iota_{Q})/\mathrm{M}_{\omega}^2$.

assumptions: the iterates remain bounded, i.e., the condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene} is satisfied

nodes.name: Global convergence of BCD-G algorithms
nodes.statement: In BCD-GLU, BCD-GQU and BCD-GU algorithms for cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}, if the iterates remain bounded, i.e., the condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene} is satisfied, then the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ converge to a point $\matr{\omega}_{*}$.
assumptions: In BCD-GLU, BCD-GQU and BCD-GU algorithms for cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}
the iterates remain bounded, i.e., the condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene} is satisfied
conclusions: the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ converge to a point $\matr{\omega}_{*}$
nodes.label: theorem_main_global_conv

nodes.name: Proof of global convergence of BCD-G
nodes.statement: We first prove the case of BCD-GLU algorithm. By \Cref{lemma:global_rho_c,lemma:global_rho_c-2}, we see that \begin{equation} g(\matr{X}_{k-1})-g(\matr{X}_{k})\geq\min(\sigma_{D},\sigma_{LU})\|\ProjGrad{g}{\matr{X}_{k-1}}\|\|\matr{X}_{k}-\matr{X}_{k-1}\|, \end{equation} whenever the elementary function $h_k=h^{(D)}_{k}, h^{(U)}_{k}$ or $h^{(L)}_k$. By the above inequality \cref{equation-condition-weak_c-5-0-proof-7.1} and \Cref{lemma:line_search}, we have that \begin{equation} f(\matr{\omega}_{k-1})-f(\matr{\omega}_{k})\geq\min(\sigma_{D},\sigma_{LU},\sigma_{p})\|\ProjGrad{f_{t_k}}{\matr{\omega}_{k-1}}\|\|\matr{\omega}_{k}-\matr{\omega}_{k-1}\| \end{equation} always holds in BCD-GLU algorithm, which is the inequality \cref{eq:sufficient_descent-2} in \Cref{theorem-SU15-2}, if we set $\sigma=\min(\sigma_{D},\sigma_{LU},\sigma_{p})$. Therefore, if $\matr{\omega}_*$ is an accumulation point of the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ produced by BCD-GLU algorithms, it is the limit point. Note that the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ remain bounded by condition \cref{eq:condi_bounded_X_gene}. There exists an accumulation point $\matr{\omega}_*$ such that the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ converge to $\matr{\omega}_{*}$. For other two cases of BCD-GQU and BCD-GU algorithms, by \Cref{lemma:line_search}, \Cref{lemma:global_rho_c}, \Cref{lemma:global_rho_c-2} and \Cref{lemma:h_k_condition_SU}, we can similarly prove that the inequality \cref{eq:sufficient_descent-2} is always satisfied, if we set $\sigma=\min(\sigma_{D},\sigma_{LU},\sigma_{Q},\sigma_{p})$ and $\min(\sigma_{D},\sigma_{LU},\sigma_{p})$, respectively. The proof is complete.

nodes.name: Proof of weak convergence of BCD-G
nodes.statement: We first prove the case of BCD-GLU algorithm. By \Cref{lemma:weak_rho_inequality_c}, we see that \begin{equation} g(\matr{X}_{k-1})-g(\matr{X}_{k})\geq\min(\eta_{D},\eta_{LU})\|\ProjGrad{g}{\matr{X}_{k-1}}\|^2, \end{equation} whenever the elementary function $h_k=h^{(D)}_{k}, h^{(U)}_{k}$ or $h^{(L)}_k$. By the above inequality \cref{equation-condition-weak_c-5-0-proof-7.1-43} and \Cref{lemma:line_search-2}, we have that \begin{equation} f(\matr{\omega}_{k-1})-f(\matr{\omega}_{k})\geq\min(\eta_{D},\eta_{LU},\eta_{p})\|\ProjGrad{f_{t_k}}{\matr{\omega}_{k-1}}\|^2 \end{equation} always holds in BCD-GLU algorithm, which is the inequality \cref{equation-condition-weak_c} in \Cref{theorem-weak-general_c}, if we set $\eta=\min(\eta_{D},\eta_{LU},\eta_{p})$. Therefore, if $\matr{\omega}_*$ is an accumulation point of the iterates $\{\matr{\omega}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ produced by BCD-GLU algorithm, then $\matr{\omega}_*$ is a stationary point. For other two cases of BCD-GQU and BCD-GU algorithms, by \Cref{lemma:weak_rho_inequality_c} and \Cref{lemma:weak_rho_inequality_c-4}, we can similarly prove that the inequality \cref{equation-condition-weak_c} is always satisfied, if we set $\eta=\min(\eta_{D},\eta_{LU},\eta_{Q},\eta_{p})$ and $\min(\eta_{D},\eta_{LU},\eta_{p})$, respectively. The proof is complete.

nodes.name: Jacobi-GLU-M and Jacobi-GQU-M variants
nodes.statement: We propose two natural variants of Jacobi-GLU and Jacobi-GQU algorithms, which will be called \emph{Jacobi-GLU-M} and \emph{Jacobi-GQU-M} algorithms, respectively. In these two algorithms, in each iteration, among all the index pairs $(i_k,j_k)$ and elementary functions $h_k$ satisfying inequality \cref{eq-inequality-G-LU_c}, we choose $(i_k,j_k)$ and $h_k$ such that the cost function obtains the largest reduction. It is clear that \Cref{theorem:weak_Jaco_Lu-0,theorem_main_weak_conv-Jacobi-GLU-09} also apply to these two new variants.
nodes.statement_short: Variants picking the pair and elementary function with largest cost reduction; the Jacobi-G convergence theorems still apply.
nodes.label: subsec:Glu-M

nodes.name: Cyclic Jacobi-CLU and Jacobi-CQU variants
nodes.statement: In Jacobi-GLU and Jacobi-GQU algorithms, a more natural way of choosing the index pair $(i_k,j_k)$ is according to a \emph{cyclic} ordering. In fact, this cyclic way has often been used in the literature \cite{maurandi2014decoupled,sorensen2009approximate,wang2012complex}. In this case, we call them the \emph{Jacobi-CLU} and \emph{Jacobi-CQU} algorithms, respectively.
nodes.label: remar:jacobi-c

nodes.name: Experiments with BCD-GLU and BCD-GQU
nodes.statement: For the following sets of complex matrices, we run BCD-GLU and BCD-GQU algorithms to minimize the cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi}. The values of cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-0-equi} in the iterations are shown in \Cref{figure-example-1-1}. The positive constant $\upsilon$ in inequality \cref{eq:inequality_BCD_G} is fixed to $0.001$. For the positive constant $\varepsilon$ in inequality \cref{eq-inequality-G-LU_c}, we choose different values. For example, \emph{BCD-GLU 0.5} means the BCD-GLU algorithm with $\varepsilon=0.5\sqrt{\frac{2}{3m(m-1)}}$. If $\varepsilon=0$, we denote the BCD-GLU and BCD-GQU algorithms by BCD-CLU and BCD-CQU, respectively. The starting point is $\matr{\omega}_{0}=(\matr{I}_{n\times m},\matr{I}_{m})$. \\ (i) We set $n=5$, $m=3$, and randomly generate complex matrices $\{\matr{A}_{\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq 3}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{5\times 5}$.\\ (ii) We set $n=10$, $m=8$, randomly generate a complex matrix $\matr{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{10\times 10}$, and set $\matr{A}^{(\ell)}=\matr{X}^{\sf H} (\matr{I}_{10}+\vect{e}_{\ell}^{{\sf T}}\vect{e}_{\ell})\matr{X}$ for $1\leq \ell\leq 5$.\\ (iii) We set $n=10$, $m=8$, randomly generate a complex upper triangular matrix $\matr{X}\in\mathbf{UT}_{10}(\mathbb{C})$, complex diagonal matrices $\{\matr{D}_{\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq 5}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{10\times 10}$, and set $\matr{A}^{(\ell)}=\matr{X}^{\sf H} \matr{D}_{\ell} \matr{X}$ for $1\leq \ell\leq 5$. \\ (iv) We set $n=10$, $m=8$, randomly generate a complex nonsingular matrix $\matr{X}\in\mathbf{SL}_{10}(\mathbb{C})$, complex diagonal matrices $\{\matr{D}_{\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq 5}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{10\times 10}$, and set $\matr{A}^{(\ell)}=\matr{X}^{\sf H} \matr{D}_{\ell} \matr{X}$ for $1\leq \ell\leq 5$.
nodes.statement_short: BCD-GLU/GQU with several ε on four random JADM instances, compared with cyclic BCD-CLU/CQU.
nodes.label: example-1-1

nodes.name: Experiments with Jacobi-type algorithms
nodes.statement: For the following sets of complex matrices, we run eight Jacobi-type algorithms to minimize the cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-1}. Here, we denote by Jacobi-GQ the gradient-based Jacobi-type algorithm on the unitary group proposed in \cite{ULC2019}, and by Jacobi-CQ the Jacobi-type algorithm on the unitary group with a cyclic ordering. Note that Jacobi-GQ and Jacobi-CQ find the iterates only in $\UNN{m}(\mathbb{C})$, not in $\mathbf{SL}_m(\mathbb{C})$. The values of cost function \cref{eq:sym_tensor_diagonalization-gener-1} in the iterations are shown in \Cref{figure-example-1}. We choose the starting point $\matr{X}_{0}=\matr{I}_{m}$.\\ (i) We randomly generate two complex matrices $\{\matr{A}_{\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq 2}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{5\times 5}$.\\ (ii) We randomly generate a complex matrix $\matr{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{10\times 10}$, and set $\matr{A}^{(\ell)}=\matr{X}^{\sf H} (\matr{I}_{10}+\vect{e}_{\ell}^{{\sf T}}\vect{e}_{\ell})\matr{X}$ for $1\leq \ell\leq 10$.
nodes.statement_short: Eight Jacobi-type algorithms on SL_m and the unitary group on two random instances.
nodes.label: example-1

nodes.name: Numerical comparison of the algorithms
nodes.statement: From the above numerical experiments, we can see that: (i) in \Cref{example-1-1}, compared with BCD-GLU algorithms, the BCD-GQU algorithms generally have better performances; (ii) in \Cref{example-1}, compared with Jacobi-GQU algorithms, the Jacobi-GLU algorithms generally have better performances; (iii) in \Cref{example-1}, compared with the Jacobi-GQ and Jacobi-CQ algorithms on $\UNN{m}(\mathbb{C})$, the Jacobi-type algorithms on $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ considered in this paper always obtain much smaller cost function values, and they also need more iterations to attain steady state values of cost functions.
conclusions: the BCD-GQU algorithms generally have better performances
the Jacobi-GLU algorithms generally have better performances
the Jacobi-type algorithms on $\mathbf{SL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ considered in this paper always obtain much smaller cost function values

nodes.name: Guaranteeing bounded iterates together with the descent inequalities
nodes.statement: An interesting question is, in the BCD-G and Jacobi-G algorithms, whether one can find a method to guarantee both the boundedness of the iterates and the inequalities \cref{eq:sufficient_descent-2,equation-condition-weak_c} for global and weak convergence.
